evidence: Engagement rate is nearly identical dataset-wide (~19.9%) regardless of platform, content type, category, sponsorship, or creator size (Phase 0 finding).

Confirmed at the most detailed level tested (platform x content type x category x creator size): differences are at most 1% from the platform average, well under our 5% threshold for a real difference.
Reach (views) does not scale with creator size: typical post gets ~10,100 views whether the creator has 126K or 874K followers.
Sponsored vs. organic posts across 60 matched groups (platform x creator size x category) differ by at most ~0.7pp either way -- no sponsorship effect detected.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Creator size (Small/Mid/Large/Mega, based on follower count) makes no meaningful difference to engagement rate on any platform -- the biggest gap between size tiers on the same platform is about 0.2%. Reach (views) is also flat across creator sizes.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: On Bilibili, evening posts score about 0.1% above the platform average engagement rate, and night posts score about 0.1% below -- essentially no difference between times of day.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: On Instagram, evening posts score about 0.1% above the platform average engagement rate, about the same as night posts -- essentially no difference between times of day.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Content length (short/medium/long, measured separately within each content type) makes no meaningful difference to engagement rate -- less than 5% difference in every case.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Number of hashtags used makes no meaningful difference to engagement rate once compared within the same platform -- the biggest gap between hashtag-count groups is about 0.2%.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Even the single best-performing detailed segment found (text posts about beauty from small creators on RedNote) only reaches 0.9% above the platform average engagement rate (85 posts) -- below the 5% bar we use to call something a real difference.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Even the single best-performing detailed segment found (text posts about tech from mega creators on YouTube) only reaches 0.9% above the platform average engagement rate (47 posts) -- below the 5% bar we use to call something a real difference.

findings.question: Q4
findings.claim: Even the single worst-performing detailed segment found (mixed-format beauty posts from mega creators on RedNote) sits only 1.0% below the platform average engagement rate (111 posts) -- below the 5% bar, so no detailed segment qualifies as a genuine underperformer.

findings.question: Q4
findings.claim: Even the single worst-performing detailed segment found (text posts about tech from small creators on Bilibili) sits only 0.8% below the platform average engagement rate (51 posts) -- below the 5% bar, so no detailed segment qualifies as a genuine underperformer.

findings.question: Q4
findings.claim: The worst-performing 10% of posts (5,222 posts) include slightly more posts from small creators than the rest of the dataset (about 1 percentage point more) -- a weak pattern worth watching, not a proven cause.
findings.method: comparison of worst 10% vs rest of dataset
findings.technical_detail: decile comparison of category shares; +1.2pp vs rest of dataset
findings.usage_guidance: Treat as a hypothesis to test, not a rule to act on. Do not cut sponsorship budget for small creators or change size targeting based on this alone -- validate with a controlled test before changing spend or strategy.

findings.question: Q2
findings.claim: Comparing sponsored to organic posts across 60 matched groups (same platform, creator size, and category), sponsored posts perform essentially the same as organic -- the difference ranges from 0.7% lower to 0.6% higher, typically 0%. This holds after matching, so it is not an artifact of comparing unlike groups: sponsorship shows no meaningful engagement lift or penalty in this dataset.
findings.method: statistical test across matched groups, median of group differences
findings.effect_size: range across 60 groups: ~1.2pp end to end
findings.technical_detail: Mann-Whitney U per stratum; lift span 0.993x-1.006x; 3% of strata p<0.05

findings.question: Q2
findings.claim: Even in the single group most favorable to sponsorship found (Instagram, large creators, tech category), sponsored posts scored only 0.6% higher than organic (517 posts) -- not a reliable difference. No platform/creator-size/category combination shows sponsorship clearly paying off in this dataset.

findings.question: Q2
findings.claim: Even in the single group least favorable to sponsorship found (TikTok, mega creators, tech category), sponsored posts scored only 0.7% lower than organic (512 posts) -- this is not strong evidence that sponsorship hurts engagement either.

findings.question: Q2
findings.claim: How a sponsorship is disclosed (explicit vs. implicit) makes no meaningful difference to engagement rate once compared within the same platform -- the biggest platform-level gap is about 0.1% (largest on Instagram).

findings.question: Q3
findings.claim: Audience age makes no meaningful difference to engagement: even the best case found (Bilibili posts whose dominant audience is 50+) is only 0.1% above the platform average (516 posts) -- below the 5% bar.

findings.question: Q3
findings.claim: Audience gender skew makes no meaningful difference to engagement rate within any platform -- the biggest platform-level gap is about 0.1%.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Confirms the flat-signal pattern holds at the deepest level tested (platform x content type x category x creator size, 240 groups, n>=30 each): the full range is only 2.0 percentage points around the platform average -- not an artifact of broad averages. Reach (views) also stays flat (~10,100) across creator-size bands from 126K to 874K followers.
findings.method: global vs. detailed-segment median comparison, plus reach-vs-followers check

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Independent audit re-checked creator-size, sponsorship and reach findings from raw data: all three confirmed exactly (tier gap 1.002x, sponsorship lift 0.994x-1.006x, follower-vs-views correlation 0.005).

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Searched 6,760 narrow combos (platform, format, category, time, size, sponsorship, length; n>=30 each). Best: +1.3% vs median; worst: -1.4%. No cut is meaningful.

findings.question: Q1
findings.claim: Long videos (>60s), evening, tech, 100K+ creators (n=1019): best platform (Bilibili) reaches only +0.5% vs its usual rate.

assumptions: creator_tier = follower_count quartiles (Small/Mid/Large/Mega), approved at GATE 0.
No cost/spend column exists; 'does sponsorship pay off' is answered only via engagement lift, never $ ROI.
content_length is bucketed into quartiles WITHIN content_type because units differ (video seconds vs text/caption chars).
daypart (morning/afternoon/evening/night) derived from post_date hour; no timezone normalization available.
audience_age/gender/location columns are treated as the single dominant audience segment per post, not a full distribution.
caveats: Engagement patterns are unusually uniform across segments -- read all lifts as directional signals for discussion, not guaranteed real-market outcomes.
Groups with fewer than 30 posts are excluded; some fine-grained combos (e.g. platform x tier x category x sponsored x disclosure) were too small to report.
Significance tests are noted in technical_detail for reference only; with ~52,000 rows tiny differences can look 'significant' -- effect size, not significance, should drive decisions.
